comparator.route: Sustainable City and Safe City themes; thesis graduation track; Urban Arts, Culture and Society thesis pathway
comparator.sourceNotes: The current 2026-27 Study Guide and public product API define 60 EC in each year. Year one is a fixed 60-EC interdisciplinary and methods foundation. In year two, 30 EC of compulsory lecture and methods courses are combined with two 10-EC thematic electives and two 5-EC methodology electives. The current public programme page lists Sustainable City and Safe City first, so those themes are selected as the neutral official-order tie-break; the first two catalogue-listed methodology electives are used. Year three contains a compulsory 5-EC literature seminar, a 25-EC graduation track and 30 EC of genuine elective, minor, internship or study-abroad space. The ordinary thesis track and its first-listed Urban Arts, Culture and Society seminar, research lab and thesis options are selected rather than the alternative Urban Environmental Science project. The choices were made before and independently of UCR fit, and all components total exactly 180 EC.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target is the generic Urban Studies bachelor. The official curriculum requires two of four themes and offers a thesis or Urban Environmental Science graduation route. No route is established as uniquely primary. Sustainable City and Safe City are the first two themes on the current public programme page; the ordinary thesis route matches the programme page's standard description of completion through an interdisciplinary thesis; and the Urban Arts, Culture and Society options appear first within that route. These neutral order choices do not use UCR fit.

alternatives.label: Cities, society and governance
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum combines comparative institutions, public economics, law, sociology, urban-theme evidence, public health, communication, sustainability and mixed research methods.
alternatives.concept: A broad urban-studies programme examining how institutions, law, public finance, history, social relations, communication, health, safety and sustainability shape cities. Comparative, qualitative, quantitative and historical methods support analysis of urban change and governance.
progression: Foundations in law, comparative politics, data, public health, psychology, sociology and history precede upper-level governance, criminal justice, conflict, social theory and research. Public Economics follows Research Methods & Statistics; both law courses with formal prerequisites follow Law, Society & Justice. Every course is offered in its assigned term.

alternatives.label: Sustainable and climate-resilient cities
alternatives.labelReason: Earth systems, hazards, biodiversity, water, materials, spatial data, public economics and sustainability governance organise the curriculum around urban environmental transition and resilience.
alternatives.concept: Focuses on sustainable and climate-resilient urban systems through Earth and climate science, biodiversity, water management, material cycles, renewable systems and environmental observation. Economics, data analysis, governance and applied research connect environmental evidence to urban policy choices.
progression: Sustainability and Earth-system gateways precede system modelling, GIS, upper-level environmental science, recycling and renewable-system design. Research Methods & Statistics precedes Public Economics and Econometrics; all other formal prerequisites and term offerings pass.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the broad route, this schedule replaces most law, politics, sociology, health and communication study with a continuous sequence in Earth systems, hazards, climate, biodiversity, water, resources, renewable systems, spatial data and applied sustainability research.

alternatives.label: Safe and healthy urban communities
alternatives.labelReason: Public health, social and medical psychology, criminal justice, extremism, conflict, inequality and community research form the curriculum’s distinct urban-wellbeing and safety emphasis.
alternatives.concept: Examines urban safety and wellbeing through public health, social and medical psychology, crime and criminal justice, extremism, conflict, inequality, communication and community governance. Statistical, qualitative, data and historical methods support analysis of vulnerable and resilient urban communities.
progression: Law, data, public-health, psychology, sociology and history foundations precede criminal justice, advanced health psychology, extremism, conflict, social theory and research. Introduction to Brain & Behavior precedes Abnormal Psychology and Medical & Health Psychology; law prerequisites and all term offerings pass.
alternatives.distinctness: Against the broad route, this curriculum replaces climate change, public economics, comparative constitutional law and EU politics with brain-and-behaviour foundations, psychological statistics, abnormal psychology and medical and health psychology. The four-course change follows the healthy-city concept rather than numerical threshold filling, while the shared safety, governance and community courses preserve its urban-studies foundation.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Comparative and interdisciplinary understanding of cities, urbanisation and urban life
Urban governance, planning, history, public policy and political economy
Cultural diversity, citizenship, belonging, migration, language, gender and inequality in cities
Sustainable, safe, multicultural and healthy city themes
Academic writing, qualitative and quantitative research, statistics and spatial analysis
Urban theory, research lab and independent thesis
adjacent: Climate resilience, environmental policy, circular material flows and urban biodiversity
Crime, violence, policing, safety and governance
Multicultural, multilingual and unequal urban communities
Public health, wellbeing, pollution and behaviour in urban settings
questions: How do institutions, social relations and historical change shape cities and urban life?
How can cities become environmentally sustainable and climate resilient?
How can urban communities become safer and healthier without deepening inequality?

selection.assessment: Three evidence-backed UCR programmes are feasible and pairwise distinct by at least four courses: a broad cities, society and governance route; a sustainable and climate-resilient cities route; and a safe and healthy urban communities route. Cultural diversity and the multicultural-city direction are substantively covered by the broad route rather than manufactured as a fourth programme.

blocks: Urban governance, history, law and political economy
Both examine institutions and public authority; UCR is comparative politics rather than a dedicated urban-governance course.
Both address law, justice and social responses to harm; Leiden focuses specifically on crime and criminalisation in the city.
Criminal law and justice provide a direct institutional lens on the Safe City theme, without reproducing its full urban scope.
Both analyse multi-actor governance and policy choices around spatial development; UCR focuses on sustainability governance.
Leiden's programme-specific Urban Studies foundation has no single UCR course counterpart.
The programme-specific Reading the City component has no sufficiently direct UCR counterpart.
Urban communities, diversity, safety and health
Both study social groups, inequality and community structure; Leiden applies these specifically to urban cultural diversity.
Both examine social determinants of behaviour; Leiden embeds them in Urban Studies.
Both study how communication constructs public meaning, while Leiden focuses on representations of the city.
Both analyse language, power and identity; Leiden applies them to multicultural and multilingual cities.
Both engage advanced social theory and civil society; Leiden's seminar is explicitly centred on urban theory and philosophy.
Both develop qualitative research design and interpretation.
Both address population health and wellbeing; Leiden places the topic specifically in cities.
Both develop inferential statistical analysis; UCR does so through psychological research.
Both examine climate change, impacts and adaptation; Leiden integrates these within the Sustainable City theme.
Both address biodiversity and governance; Leiden's elective is specifically about biodiversity in cities.
Both use spatial analysis and modelling; UCR emphasises GIS and Earth-observation data.
Both examine material flows, reuse and environmental impacts; UCR focuses on recovery and remediation.
Academic skills, methods, research and open space
Both develop academic writing, presentation and collaborative skills; UCR also includes personal and professional development.
Both introduce research design and quantitative methods.
The urban-humanities methodology elective has no sufficiently direct UCR course counterpart.
The selected programme-specific thesis seminar has no ordinary UCR course counterpart.
The selected programme-specific Urban Studies research lab has no ordinary UCR course counterpart.
Leiden's compulsory 10-EC Urban Studies thesis remains distinct from ordinary UCR courses and from UCR's optional research opportunity.
The genuine 30-EC elective, minor, internship or study-abroad space remains open and is not treated as fixed urban content.

notes.text: Leiden offers an integrated Urban Studies sequence with city-specific foundations, thematic lectures, electives, methods, a research lab and a compulsory thesis. UCR can construct three coherent urban-focused programmes from governance, sociology, law, health, sustainability, environmental science and research methods, but it does not reproduce the same dedicated Urban Studies core; shared rows indicate substantive overlap rather than course equivalence.
